readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Manuel’s treachery
readings.challenge: Track the gap between what Buck assumes and what the narrator lets the reader see.
readings.focus: A proud dog meets force for the first time, and men price him like goods.
readings.context: The Call of the Wild (1903) by Jack London follows Buck, a big dog stolen from a California judge’s estate in 1897 and sold into the Klondike gold rush, where he hauls sleds and learns to survive. Buck has lived four years as the Judge’s favorite; Manuel, a gardener’s helper, needs money for his gambling. A flag station is a stop where trains halt only when signalled. ’Frisco is San Francisco; “hydrophoby” is hydrophobia, or rabies; to “pull your freight” is to leave.
readings.contentNote: A dog is choked unconscious and a man’s hand is badly bitten. The saloon-keeper uses “squarehead,” an old insulting nickname for Scandinavian and German immigrants.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Into the Primitive,” from the night of Manuel’s treachery to the saloon-keeper’s laugh; opens “The Judge was at a meeting of the Raisin Growers' Association, and the boys were busy…”; closes “…laughed the saloon-keeper. "Here, lend me a hand before you pull your freight," he added.”.

questions.prompt: Buck “imagined” the walk was merely a stroll and believed that “to intimate was to command.” What do these phrases show about the limits of what Buck knows?
facilitatorNotes: He reads the world through his life at the Judge’s, where men he knew could be trusted and a growl was obeyed. The narrator knows more than Buck and lets the reader see the danger first.
evidence: what Buck imagined was merely a stroll
in his pride believing that to intimate was to command

questions.prompt: How do the men talk about Buck? Find words that turn him into merchandise.
facilitatorNotes: He is “the goods” to be wrapped and delivered, and the talk in the saloon is all prices. Their language makes a proud animal into a parcel, which sharpens the reader’s sense of outrage.
evidence: You might wrap up the goods before you deliver 'm
That makes a hundred and fifty

questions.prompt: The narrator gives Buck “the unbridled anger of a kidnapped king.” Is the phrase admiring, comic, or both?
facilitatorNotes: It honors his pride and courage, and carries over his life as master of the Judge’s estate. Some readers also hear a mock-heroic joke: grand royal words for a dog in a baggage car. Both readings fit.
evidence: the unbridled anger of a kidnapped king

questions.prompt: “The man spoke most eloquently for himself.” What is ironic about the sentence, and what do the bloody handkerchief and ripped trouser leg tell us?
facilitatorNotes: His “eloquence” is grumbling, and his wounds speak louder than his words: they tell the story of Buck’s fight on the train. The narrator lets the evidence describe the struggle instead of narrating it.
evidence: the man spoke most eloquently for himself
I wouldn't do it over for a thousand, cold cash.

readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: The raid at Lake Le Barge
readings.challenge: Keep track of a fast, crowded fight, and of the conflict it interrupts.
readings.focus: A secret rivalry flares up, and hunger turns starving huskies into a force of nature.
readings.context: The Call of the Wild (1903) by Jack London follows Buck, a big dog stolen from a California judge’s estate in 1897 and sold into the Klondike gold rush, where he hauls sleds and learns to survive. Buck now pulls on a mail team driven by two French-Canadian couriers, Perrault and François, and has learned “the law of club and fang.” Spitz, the lead dog, has bullied him from the start. Dyea is the port where the trail began, and Dawson the gold-rush town the team is bound for. “By Gar” and “sacredam” are François’s oaths.
readings.contentNote: Dogs fight savagely and are badly wounded; one dog’s leg is crushed and its neck broken. The huskies are said to come from an “Indian village,” in the period’s terms.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “The Dominant Primordial Beast,” from the opening to the wound-stiffened team setting out again; opens “THE dominant primordial beast was strong in Buck, and under the fierce conditions of…”; closes “…trail they had yet encountered, and for that matter, the hardest between them and Dawson.”.

questions.prompt: The chapter calls the beast in Buck “a secret growth.” How does he treat Spitz at first, and what finally breaks his restraint?
facilitatorNotes: He avoids fights and shows no impatience, so Spitz takes him for a timid dog. When Spitz steals his warm nest, “the beast in him roared”: a small insult releases what has been building.
evidence: Yet it was a secret growth.
The beast in him roared.

questions.prompt: Why does François cheer for Buck in this fight?
facilitatorNotes: He sees what happened at the nest and calls Spitz the thief. The driver judges by fairness, which shows that the men watch the dogs’ quarrels closely and take sides.
evidence: Gif it to heem, the dirty t'eef!

questions.prompt: How does London make hunger, rather than the huskies themselves, the real enemy in this raid?
facilitatorNotes: They ignore the clubs until the last crumb is gone and even eat moccasins, traces and a whip lash. They are skeletons, made “irresistible” by “hunger-madness.” Some readers pity them; others see only menace. The text supports both.
evidence: But the hunger-madness made them terrifying, irresistible.
nothing, no matter how remotely eatable, had escaped them

questions.prompt: In the middle of the raid, Spitz attacks Buck from the side. What does this add to their rivalry, and why does the narrator say the raid pushed their struggle “far into the future”?
facilitatorNotes: Spitz uses the chaos to try to kill Buck, which shows his treachery. The raid postpones the decisive fight across “many a weary mile,” so the reader now expects it.
evidence: It was Spitz, treacherously attacking from the side.
past many a weary mile of trail and toil

readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Dolly’s madness and the pride of the trail
readings.challenge: Hold together a breathless chase, two drivers’ predictions and a long paragraph that reflects on pride.
readings.focus: What makes Buck dangerous, and why dogs love the work that may kill them.
readings.context: The Call of the Wild (1903) by Jack London follows Buck, a big dog stolen from a California judge’s estate in 1897 and sold into the Klondike gold rush, where he hauls sleds and learns to survive. On the trail to Dawson, starving huskies have mauled the team, and François fears their bites will cause madness. Spitz, the lead dog, and Buck have hated each other from the start. The Pelly is a river on the Yukon route. The man in the red sweater beat Buck with a club when he was first sold. A wheel-dog runs nearest the sled; “Southland” dogs come from the warm south.
readings.contentNote: A mad dog is killed with an axe; Spitz tears Buck’s flesh while he is helpless; a dog is whipped.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “The Dominant Primordial Beast,” from Dolly’s madness at the Pelly to “And this was Buck’s pride, too.”; opens “At the Pelly one morning, as they were harnessing up, Dolly, who had never been…”; closes “…pride that made him fear Buck as a possible lead-dog. And this was Buck's pride, too.”.

questions.prompt: During the chase, Dolly cannot gain on Buck “so great was his terror,” and he cannot leave her “so great was her madness.” How does the sentence’s balance capture the chase?
facilitatorNotes: Two matching clauses lock the dogs together, always one leap apart, until François breaks the deadlock with the axe. The shape of the sentence acts out the stalemate.
evidence: nor could she gain on him, so great was his terror, nor could he leave her, so great was her madness

questions.prompt: Perrault calls Spitz “one devil”; François calls Buck “two devils.” What does François see that Perrault does not?
facilitatorNotes: He has watched Buck and believes that his patience hides a greater ferocity that will one day break out. The comic dialect carries a real judgment, which the narrator goes on to confirm.
evidence: Dat Buck two devils
All de tam I watch dat Buck I know for sure.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator say the club of the man in the red sweater made Buck more dangerous, not less?
facilitatorNotes: The beating taught him that rashness loses. His ambition is now controlled and patient: a lesson in submission became a lesson in strategy.
evidence: had knocked all blind pluck and rashness out of his desire for mastery
could bide his time with a patience that was nothing less than primitive

questions.prompt: The “pride of the trail and trace” can make dogs “die joyfully in the harness.” Is London praising this pride, questioning it, or both?
facilitatorNotes: He admires how it turns “sour and sullen brutes” into eager workers, but it also exhausts them, breaks their hearts, drives Spitz’s punishments and fuels the rivalry. Readers may weigh these differently; the repetition of “pride” makes it seem a force beyond choosing.
evidence: which lures them to die joyfully in the harness, and breaks their hearts if they are cut out of the harness
transforming them from sour and sullen brutes into straining, eager, ambitious creatures

readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: An open mutiny
readings.challenge: Follow a power struggle carried on by indirect means, and notice where the narrator’s admiration for Buck stops.
readings.focus: Buck undermines the leader’s authority, and the team falls apart.
readings.context: Recap: after mad Dolly chased him and Spitz attacked him while he lay exhausted, Buck and Spitz are at war over who will lead the team. Pike is a “malingerer,” a dog that fakes illness to avoid work. The Barracks housed the North-West Mounted Police at Dawson; “Salt Water” is the coast; the aurora borealis is the northern lights.
readings.contentNote: Dogs fight, and Buck is beaten with the butt of a whip.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “The Dominant Primordial Beast,” from Buck’s open threat to Spitz’s leadership to the tangled traces; opens “He openly threatened the other's leadership. He came between him and the shirks he should…”; closes “…a greater delight slyly to precipitate a fight amongst his mates and tangle the traces.”.

questions.prompt: How does Buck challenge Spitz without fighting him directly? Why is this more dangerous to Spitz than a fight?
facilitatorNotes: He protects the dogs Spitz should punish, so the others lose their fear of the leader. Authority that depends on fear cannot survive that, and Buck learns to do it when François is not watching.
evidence: He came between him and the shirks he should have punished. And he did it deliberately.
but he did it craftily, when François was not around

questions.prompt: François is “chuckling at the incident while unswerving in the administration of justice.” What do the two attitudes together say about him?
facilitatorNotes: He enjoys Buck’s spirit but enforces order for the team’s sake. The courtroom words are a joke about a dog-driver acting as judge, and they also show he understands what is at stake.
evidence: chuckling at the incident while unswerving in the administration of justice

questions.prompt: In Dawson the huskies’ nightly song is “the pleading of life.” What does the song mean to Buck, and why might London place it between scenes of mutiny?
facilitatorNotes: It connects Buck with “the pain of his wild fathers,” a pull deeper than the quarrel over leadership. Placed in the middle of the power struggle, it widens the frame from a team’s fight to the ancient struggle to live.
evidence: more the pleading of life, the articulate travail of existence
harked back through the ages of fire and roof to the raw beginnings of life

questions.prompt: By the end, Buck’s “conduct approached that of a bully.” Does the narrator want us on Buck’s side here? Use evidence.
facilitatorNotes: He admires Buck’s cleverness and plainly records its cost: the team’s solidarity is destroyed and the camp becomes a “howling bedlam.” Students can argue that the narrator admires Buck’s rise, or that he presents it with some unease.
evidence: his conduct approached that of a bully
The insidious revolt led by Buck had destroyed the solidarity of the team.

readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Sold for a song at Skaguay
readings.challenge: Separate two kinds of tiredness, and notice how quickly the narrator judges the new owners.
readings.focus: The cost of a record mail run, and the arrival of people out of place in the North.
readings.context: The Call of the Wild (1903) by Jack London follows Buck, a big dog stolen from a California judge’s estate in 1897 and sold into the Klondike gold rush, where he hauls sleds and learns to survive. Buck has become lead dog of the mail team, which has run from Dawson to the coast at Skaguay in record time. Now the mail service is replacing its worn-out dogs. “Mush” is a driver’s command to go; Hudson Bay dogs are fresh northern sled dogs; “chaffering” is haggling; callowness is youthful inexperience.
readings.contentNote: The narrator calls the team’s driver a “Scotch half-breed,” an offensive period term for a person of mixed Scottish and Indigenous descent.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “The Toil of Trace and Trail,” from the mail team’s arrival at Skaguay to “a nice family party”; opens “THIRTY days from the time it left Dawson, the Salt Water Mail, with Buck and his mates at…”; closes “…the men called her. She was Charles's wife and Hal's sister—a nice family party.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator separates two kinds of “dead-tiredness.” What is the difference, and why does it matter for these dogs?
facilitatorNotes: One comes from brief, excessive effort and passes in hours; the other comes from months of slow drain and leaves no reserve at all. The numbers (twenty-five hundred miles, five days’ rest in the last eighteen hundred) show which kind this is.
evidence: the dead-tiredness that comes through the slow and prolonged strength drainage of months of toil
There was no power of recuperation left

questions.prompt: “Since dogs count for little against dollars, they were to be sold.” Whose decision is this, and how does the narrator want us to judge it?
facilitatorNotes: It comes from official orders, driven by the mail piling up in the gold rush. The short, dry phrase sets money against the “common justice” the drivers and dogs have earned, and invites the reader to judge it harshly.
evidence: dogs count for little against dollars
in the nature of reason and common justice they deserved an interval of loafing

questions.prompt: Which details make Charles and Hal seem “out of place”? Choose the one you find most revealing.
facilitatorNotes: Charles’s fierce mustache “giving the lie” to a weak lip; Hal’s cartridge belt that “advertised his callowness.” The narrator reads appearance as character. Readers may ask whether such quick judgments are fair, though the messy camp seems to bear them out.
evidence: giving the lie to the limply drooping lip it concealed
It advertised his callowness

questions.prompt: The passage ends with “a nice family party.” What is the tone, and what does the camp suggest about what is coming?
facilitatorNotes: It is dry irony: nothing about the camp is nice or orderly. The half-pitched tent and unwashed dishes forecast the mismanagement to come.
evidence: a nice family party
tent half stretched, dishes unwashed, everything in disorder

readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Wayfarers to death
readings.challenge: Follow a slow collapse and notice where the narrator’s sympathy lies and where it is withdrawn.
readings.focus: Incompetence, quarrels and starvation, set against a spring the travellers cannot see.
readings.context: The Call of the Wild (1903) by Jack London follows Buck, a big dog stolen from a California judge’s estate in 1897 and sold into the Klondike gold rush, where he hauls sleds and learns to survive. Buck and his teammates have been sold to Hal, Charles and Mercedes, newcomers from the States who overloaded the sled, overfed and then starved the dogs, and do not understand the trail. “Outside” dogs are dogs brought in from outside the North; the Five Fingers are rapids on the Yukon.
readings.contentNote: Dogs starve, are beaten, and are killed with a revolver and an axe; their suffering is described directly. The narrator’s comments on Mercedes rely on period ideas about women, and an Indigenous woman is called by an offensive period term.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “The Toil of Trace and Trail,” from “The first to go was Dub” to the travellers staggering through the spring; opens “The first to go was Dub. Poor blundering thief that he was, always getting caught and…”; closes “…breezes, like wayfarers to death, staggered the two men, the woman, and the huskies.”.

questions.prompt: What starts the family’s quarrels, and how far do the quarrels wander? Why does London make them comic in the middle of so much suffering?
facilitatorNotes: A dispute over who should chop firewood drags in relatives, art, politics and the dead. The satire exposes their self-absorption, and the last sentence shows its cost. The comedy sharpens the judgment rather than softening it.
evidence: Starting from a dispute as to which should chop a few sticks for the fire
In the meantime the fire remained unbuilt, the camp half pitched, and the dogs unfed.

questions.prompt: The narrator praises “the wonderful patience of the trail,” which never comes to these three. What is it, and what replaces it?
facilitatorNotes: Hard toil makes some people kinder and gentler in speech; misery makes these three sharp-tongued. The contrast suggests that character, not hardship alone, decides how people behave.
evidence: which comes to men who toil hard and suffer sore, and remain sweet of speech and kindly
hard words were first on their lips in the morning and last at night

questions.prompt: How does London portray Mercedes? Where do you see the narrator’s own assumptions about women, and do they affect how fair the portrait is?
facilitatorNotes: Her riding on the sled is a real cruelty to starving dogs. But phrases such as “the grievance of sex” mock her through period ideas about what women expect. Readers can judge her selfish and still notice the narrator’s scorn.
evidence: Mercedes nursed a special grievance—the grievance of sex.
she weighed one hundred and twenty pounds—a lusty last straw

questions.prompt: “It was heartbreaking, only Buck’s heart was unbreakable. The man in the red sweater had proved that.” How does this connect Buck’s survival to the start of his journey?
facilitatorNotes: The first beating taught him the law of the club, and it also showed that his spirit could not be broken. He endures this suffering without accepting it.
evidence: only Buck's heart was unbreakable

questions.prompt: The last two paragraphs describe spring at length. Why end with “awakening life,” and what does “like wayfarers to death” do to that picture?
facilitatorNotes: New life returns everywhere, but neither dogs nor people notice. The thawing river also warns of danger ahead. The irony places a march toward death inside a season of rebirth.
evidence: It was beautiful spring weather, but neither dogs nor humans were aware of it.
like wayfarers to death

readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: A thing of the wild by Thornton’s fire
readings.challenge: Hold two sides of Buck in mind at once, and judge a test and a fight that reveal them.
readings.focus: Love for one man and the pull of the wild live side by side in Buck.
readings.context: The Call of the Wild (1903) by Jack London follows Buck, a big dog stolen from a California judge’s estate in 1897 and sold into the Klondike gold rush, where he hauls sleds and learns to survive. After John Thornton saved him from a brutal owner, Buck has come to love Thornton as he loved no earlier master. Skeet and Nig are Thornton’s other dogs; Hans and Pete are his partners; to grub-stake is to supply food and gear for a prospecting trip; a tenderfoot is a newcomer; a miners’ meeting was a gold camp’s court.
readings.contentNote: Buck tears open a man’s throat in a saloon fight, and the passage describes fighting without mercy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “For the Love of a Man,” from “But in spite of this great love” to Buck’s fame after the fight at Circle City; opens “But in spite of this great love he bore John Thornton, which seemed to bespeak the soft…”; closes “…his reputation was made, and from that day his name spread through every camp in Alaska.”.

questions.prompt: Buck will not steal from Thornton but steals from anyone else. What does this rule show about how his love and his wildness live side by side?
facilitatorNotes: Love makes one exception and leaves the rest of his wildness untouched. Devotion is “born of fire and roof,” while his cunning belongs to the wild; he is a wild creature visiting a fire.
evidence: Because of his very great love, he could not steal from this man
He was a thing of the wild, come in from the wild to sit by John Thornton's fire

questions.prompt: “Mercy did not exist in the primordial life. It was misunderstood for fear.” Whose view is this: Buck’s, the narrator’s, or both?
facilitatorNotes: It is the law Buck has learned, and the narrator’s strong voice seems to endorse it as a law of nature. Readers can test it against Thornton, whose mercy saved Buck’s life.
evidence: Mercy did not exist in the primordial life. It was misunderstood for fear
Kill or be killed, eat or be eaten, was the law

questions.prompt: What are the “shades” that sit behind Buck at the fire? How does this paragraph change our sense of who Buck is?
facilitatorNotes: Generations of dogs and wolves share his senses, moods and dreams, so he is both one dog and a whole line of ancestors. The long sentence piles up its phrases the way the call itself keeps pulling.
evidence: He was older than the days he had seen and the breaths he had drawn.
becoming themselves the stuff of his dreams

questions.prompt: Thornton tests Buck at the cliff edge on “a thoughtless whim.” What does he learn, and why is it “splendid” and “terrible” at once?
facilitatorNotes: Buck would leap to his death on command. Such devotion is admirable and frightening, because it gives Thornton a power he must never misuse. Some readers also judge Thornton harshly for making the test at all.
evidence: A thoughtless whim seized Thornton
No, it is splendid, and it is terrible, too.

questions.prompt: The miners’ meeting decides that Buck had “sufficient provocation.” Do you agree with the verdict?
facilitatorNotes: Burton struck Thornton without warning, so Buck was defending his master; but Buck went for the throat a second time. Readers may argue that the camp’s justice values loyalty over restraint, or that the verdict is fair.
evidence: decided that the dog had sufficient provocation
Burton struck out, without warning, straight from the shoulder.

readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: A bluff called in the Eldorado
readings.challenge: Read a tense conversation for what each speaker wants, and track Thornton’s feelings through small physical signs.
readings.focus: Pride in a dog becomes a public wager that Thornton cannot afford.
readings.context: The Call of the Wild (1903) by Jack London follows Buck, a big dog stolen from a California judge’s estate in 1897 and sold into the Klondike gold rush, where he hauls sleds and learns to survive. Buck, famous across Alaska for his devotion to John Thornton, spends the winter in Dawson with Thornton and his partners, Hans and Pete. A “Bonanza King” or “Mastodon King” is a miner made rich by a claim on Bonanza or Mastodon Creek. To “break out” a sled is to free runners frozen to the snow and start it moving. Gold dust served as money in the camps.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “For the Love of a Man,” from the boasting in the Eldorado Saloon to O’Brien’s loan; opens “That winter, at Dawson, Buck performed another exploit, not so heroic, perhaps, but one…”; closes “…"Though it's little faith I'm having, John, that the beast can do the trick."”.

questions.prompt: How do the boasts climb before Thornton speaks? Why does he name a number so much larger?
facilitatorNotes: Five, six, then seven hundred pounds; Thornton leaps to a thousand. He has been pushed to defend Buck, and pride and loyalty outrun calculation.
evidence: Buck, because of his record, was the target for these men
Buck can start a thousand pounds.

questions.prompt: “His tongue had tricked him.” What does the narrator reveal about Thornton that the men in the saloon cannot see?
facilitatorNotes: Outwardly he answered “coolly”; inside he is flushed, doubtful and without the money. The narrator shows the gap between a public face and private fear.
evidence: He could feel a flush of warm blood creeping up his face. His tongue had tricked him.
John Thornton said coolly

questions.prompt: Why does Matthewson speak “slowly and deliberately, so that all could hear”? What is he doing to Thornton?
facilitatorNotes: He makes the bet public so Thornton cannot back down without shame. The sack on the bar and the loaded sled outside remove every excuse; “brutal directness” names the pressure.
evidence: slowly and deliberately, so that all could hear
with brutal directness

questions.prompt: O’Brien lends the thousand while saying he has “little faith” that Buck can do it. Why lend it at all?
facilitatorNotes: Out of friendship with an “old-time comrade,” not belief in the dog. His loyalty to Thornton mirrors Thornton’s loyalty to Buck. Some readers add that he will not let a friend be shamed in public.
evidence: Though it's little faith I'm having, John, that the beast can do the trick.
a Mastodon King and old-time comrade

readings.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: The hairy man and the call
readings.challenge: Follow a vision of a distant past and decide what it says about Buck’s present.
readings.focus: Fear as the condition of the first world, and a call that Buck obeys without reasoning.
readings.context: The Call of the Wild (1903) by Jack London follows Buck, a big dog stolen from a California judge’s estate in 1897 and sold into the Klondike gold rush, where he hauls sleds and learns to survive. Buck now lives with John Thornton at a remote camp while the men look for a lost gold mine. Since his time on the trail he has had visions by the fire of a “short-legged hairy man,” a primitive human he seems to remember from long ago. London, like many writers of his time, imagined that animals could inherit memories of their ancestors’ lives; this is fiction, not science.
readings.contentNote: London uses “niggerheads,” a period name for clumps of marsh sedge that is built on a racial slur.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Sounding of the Call,” from “The salient thing of this other world seemed fear” to the call that summons him waking or sleeping; opens “The salient thing of this other world seemed fear. When he watched the hairy man sleeping…”; closes “…something that called—called, waking or sleeping, at all times, for him to come.”.

questions.prompt: “The salient thing of this other world seemed fear.” Which details in the hairy man’s behavior support this?
facilitatorNotes: He sleeps with starts and awakenings, peers into the dark, feeds the fire, watches for danger while eating, and sleeps clinging to a tree. Every action is shaped by threat.
evidence: peer fearfully into the darkness and fling more wood upon the fire
with eyes that roved everywhere for hidden danger

questions.prompt: How does the vision present Buck and the hairy man as partners rather than master and dog? Why might that matter?
facilitatorNotes: They creep together, equally alert, and the man’s senses are as keen as Buck’s. In this older world neither rules the other, which points toward Buck’s own move away from human masters.
evidence: the pair of them
for the man heard and smelled as keenly as Buck

questions.prompt: Buck hunts for the call “as though it were a tangible thing.” What is the call, and why can he not find it by sniffing and watching?
facilitatorNotes: It is a pull from inside him, an inherited longing, not an object in the woods. The image of Buck crouching for hours to “surprise” it is almost comic. Readers may also argue it is a real sound he cannot yet place; both readings use the text.
evidence: looking for it as though it were a tangible thing
he hoped to surprise this call he could not understand

questions.prompt: The narrator says Buck “did not reason about them at all,” yet compares him to someone reading a book. Is that a contradiction?
facilitatorNotes: He reads signs and sounds with expert skill, but by instinct rather than thought. The comparison suggests a different kind of knowing, not reasoning; some readers will still find the two claims in tension.
evidence: He was impelled to do them, and did not reason about them at all.
reading signs and sounds as man may read a book
